title: Your first table: buildings
prompt_md:
Create a table named **`buildings`** with:

- `building_id` — integer primary key
- `name` — text, required, and no two buildings may share a name
- `year_built` — integer, optional

The database starts empty. Hidden tests will insert valid rows and then try to break your constraints (duplicate id, missing name, duplicate name).

example.input_md: Press **Run** to build the schema and see an ER diagram of what you created; **Check Answer** runs the hidden behavioural tests.

hints: `CREATE TABLE buildings (building_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, ...)`
`name TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE`

checks.sql: INSERT INTO buildings (building_id, name, year_built) VALUES (1, 'DuBourg Hall', 1888)
checks.msg: a valid row should insert

checks.sql: INSERT INTO buildings (building_id, name) VALUES (2, 'Ritter Hall')
checks.msg: year_built must be optional

checks.sql: INSERT INTO buildings (building_id, name) VALUES (1, 'Another Hall')
checks.msg: a duplicate building_id must be rejected (PRIMARY KEY)

checks.sql: INSERT INTO buildings (building_id, name) VALUES (3, NULL)
checks.msg: a NULL name must be rejected (NOT NULL)

checks.sql: INSERT INTO buildings (building_id, name) VALUES (4, 'Ritter Hall')
checks.msg: a duplicate name must be rejected (UNIQUE)

checks.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM buildings
checks.msg: exactly the two valid rows should remain

title: Data types and DEFAULT
prompt_md:
Create a table **`students`** with:

- `student_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY
- `first_name`, `last_name` — required text
- `gpa` — a REAL number, optional
- `status` — text, required, **defaulting to `'active'`** when not supplied
- `created_on` — text, defaulting to the current date via `DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE`
hints: `DEFAULT 'active'` goes after the type and NOT NULL.
`created_on TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE` — SQLite fills in today's date.
solution:
CREATE TABLE students (
  student_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  first_name TEXT NOT NULL,
  last_name  TEXT NOT NULL,
  gpa        REAL,
  status     TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active',
  created_on TEXT DEFAULT CURRENT_DATE
);

checks.sql: INSERT INTO students (student_id, first_name, last_name, gpa) VALUES (1, 'Ava', 'Chen', 3.5)
checks.msg: insert without status/created_on should work

checks.sql: SELECT status FROM students WHERE student_id = 1
checks.msg: status should default to 'active'

checks.sql: SELECT created_on IS NOT NULL FROM students WHERE student_id = 1
checks.msg: created_on should default to the current date

checks.sql: INSERT INTO students (student_id, first_name, last_name) VALUES (2, 'Leo', 'Park')
checks.msg: gpa must be optional

checks.sql: INSERT INTO students (student_id, first_name, last_name, status) VALUES (3, 'X', 'Y', NULL)
checks.msg: an explicit NULL status must be rejected
gpa should be declared REAL
status needs a DEFAULT

title: Employees with unique emails
prompt_md: Create **`employees`** with `employee_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, `email` (required, unique), `title` (required), `salary` INTEGER (required, must be **positive**) and `hire_date` TEXT (required).

example.input_md: Two constraints on one column are fine: `salary INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (salary > 0)`.

hints: `email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE`
Remember NOT NULL on every required column; UNIQUE alone still allows NULL.
solution:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  employee_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  email       TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  title       TEXT NOT NULL,
  salary      INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (salary > 0),
  hire_date   TEXT NOT NULL
);

title: Terms: natural vs surrogate keys
prompt_md:
Create **`terms`** with a surrogate key `term_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, plus `year` INTEGER NOT NULL and `season` TEXT NOT NULL restricted to `'Fall'` or `'Spring'`.

The natural key is (`year`, `season`): the same season of the same year must not appear twice. Enforce that with a **table-level UNIQUE** constraint.

example.input_md: `UNIQUE (year, season)` as its own line inside CREATE TABLE.

hints: Table-level constraints go after the column list: `..., UNIQUE (year, season)`.
`CHECK (season IN ('Fall', 'Spring'))`

checks.sql: INSERT INTO terms (term_id, year, season) VALUES (1, 2024, 'Fall')
checks.msg: valid term

checks.sql: INSERT INTO terms (term_id, year, season) VALUES (2, 2025, 'Spring')
checks.msg: valid term

checks.sql: INSERT INTO terms (term_id, year, season) VALUES (3, 2024, 'Fall')
checks.msg: a second Fall 2024 must be rejected (UNIQUE on year+season)

checks.sql: INSERT INTO terms (term_id, year, season) VALUES (4, 2024, 'Summer')
checks.msg: 'Summer' must be rejected

title: One-to-many with a FOREIGN KEY
prompt_md:
A department has many employees. Create **`departments`** (`department_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, `name` TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE) and **`employees`** (`employee_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, `name` TEXT NOT NULL, `department_id` INTEGER) where `employees.department_id` is a **foreign key** to `departments`. An employee may have no department (NULL allowed).

Foreign keys are enforced here (`PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`).
hints: Create the parent table first.
Inline: `REFERENCES departments(department_id)`; or table-level: `FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES departments(department_id)`.

title: Many-to-many via a junction table

A student can be in a given club only **once**: make (`student_id`, `club_id`) the composite primary key.

example.input_md: `PRIMARY KEY (student_id, club_id)` as a table-level constraint.

hints: Three tables; the junction table has two foreign keys and a composite key.
`student_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES students(student_id)`

title: ON DELETE behaviour
prompt_md:
Create three tables:

- **`courses`** (`course_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, `title` TEXT NOT NULL)
- **`sections`** (`section_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, `course_id` INTEGER NOT NULL → courses, `room` TEXT)
- **`instructors`** (`instructor_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, `name` TEXT NOT NULL); add `instructor_id` INTEGER (nullable) to `sections` → instructors

Referential actions:

- deleting a **course** deletes its sections (`ON DELETE CASCADE`)
- deleting an **instructor** keeps the sections but sets their `instructor_id` to NULL (`ON DELETE SET NULL`)

example.input_md: `course_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES courses(course_id) ON DELETE CASCADE`

hints: The action is written right after REFERENCES ...(...): `ON DELETE CASCADE` / `ON DELETE SET NULL`.
Create `instructors` before `sections` so the reference resolves.

checks.sql: INSERT INTO courses VALUES (1, 'Databases'); INSERT INTO courses VALUES (2, 'Algorithms'); INSERT INTO instructors VALUES (7, 'Dr. Chen')
checks.msg: seed

checks.sql: INSERT INTO sections (section_id, course_id, instructor_id, room) VALUES (10, 1, 7, 'A101'); INSERT INTO sections (section_id, course_id, instructor_id, room) VALUES (11, 1, 7, 'A102'); INSERT INTO sections (section_id, course_id, instructor_id, room) VALUES (12, 2, NULL, 'B200')
checks.msg: sections should insert

checks.sql: DELETE FROM courses WHERE course_id = 1
checks.msg: deleting a course should be allowed (cascade)

checks.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sections
checks.msg: the two sections of the deleted course should be gone, one should remain

checks.sql: INSERT INTO sections (section_id, course_id, instructor_id) VALUES (13, 2, 7); DELETE FROM instructors WHERE instructor_id = 7
checks.msg: deleting an instructor should be allowed (set null)

checks.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM sections WHERE section_id = 13 AND instructor_id IS NULL
checks.msg: the section should survive with instructor_id set to NULL

title: Normalise a flat registration sheet (1NF → 3NF)
prompt_md:
A registrar keeps one wide table:

```
registrations(student_id, student_name, student_email,
              course_code, course_title, dept_code, dept_name,
              grade)
```

It has update anomalies: renaming a department means touching thousands of rows. Decompose it into **third normal form**. Keep **all of the column names above** (you may add surrogate keys). Table names are up to you, but:

- student attributes live in one table keyed by `student_id`
- course attributes live in one table keyed by `course_code`
- department attributes live in their own table keyed by `dept_code`; courses reference it
- one table holds `grade` and references the student and the course

The grader inspects structure: which columns sit together, keys, and foreign keys.

example.input_md: Four tables; `student_name` must not be in the same table as `course_title`, and `dept_name` must not be stored next to `course_title`.

hints: Ask of each non-key column: what does it depend on? `dept_name` depends only on `dept_code`, so it belongs in a departments table.
The registration/grade table has a composite key (student_id, course_code) and two foreign keys.

checks.msg: a 3NF decomposition of this sheet needs at least four tables
dept_name must be kept
course_title must be kept
student_email must be kept
grade must be kept
student_name and course_title must not live in the same table
dept_name must not be stored next to course_title (transitive dependency)
student_name must not be repeated on every grade row
course_title must not be repeated on every grade row
a table keyed by student_id alone should exist
a table keyed by course_code alone should exist
a table keyed by dept_code alone should exist
courses should reference departments via dept_code
the grade table should reference students
the grade table should reference courses
the table holding grade needs a composite key (student + course)

title: Model sections and prevent double-booking
prompt_md:
Model this spec with tables named **`rooms`**, **`terms`** and **`sections`**:

- A room has `room_id` (PK) and `room_number` TEXT NOT NULL.
- A term has `term_id` (PK) and `name` TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE.
- A section has `section_id` (PK), `course_code` TEXT NOT NULL, a `term_id` (required FK), a `room_id` (optional FK), `meeting_days` TEXT NOT NULL (e.g. `'MWF'`) and `start_time` TEXT NOT NULL (`'09:00'`).
- **Business rule:** the same room cannot host two sections in the same term on the same days at the same start time.

Two sections may share a room if any of term, days or time differ. Sections with no room never clash.

example.input_md: A table-level `UNIQUE (room_id, term_id, meeting_days, start_time)` enforces the rule (NULL room_id never collides in SQLite).

hints: Think about which combination of columns must be unique to prevent a clash.
SQLite treats NULLs as distinct in UNIQUE constraints, which is exactly what you want for room-less sections.

title: Self-referencing org chart
prompt_md:
Create **`employees`** (`employee_id` INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, `name` TEXT NOT NULL, `title` TEXT NOT NULL, `manager_id` INTEGER) where `manager_id` references **`employees` itself**.

Rules:

- the top of the tree (the President) has `manager_id` NULL
- `manager_id` must point at an existing employee
- nobody can be their **own** manager (`CHECK`)
- deleting a manager must be **rejected** while they still have reports (default action)
hints: A table can reference itself; the FK target is the same table's primary key.
CHECK with NULL evaluates to NULL, which passes — so the President row is fine.
solution:
CREATE TABLE employees (
  employee_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name        TEXT NOT NULL,
  title       TEXT NOT NULL,
  manager_id  INTEGER REFERENCES employees(employee_id),
  CHECK (manager_id <> employee_id)
);

checks.msg: a chain of reports should insert

checks.msg: a manager that does not exist must be rejected

title: Spot the normal-form violation
prompt_md: A table `enrollment_grades(student_id, section_id, grade, course_title, instructor_name)` has the composite primary key (`student_id`, `section_id`). `course_title` and `instructor_name` are determined by `section_id` alone.
question_md: Which normal form does this table **violate first**, and why?
options: 1NF — a composite primary key is not allowed in first normal form
2NF — course_title and instructor_name depend on only part of the composite key (section_id), a partial dependency
None — the table is already in 3NF because every column depends on the whole key
explanation: Second normal form forbids non-key columns that depend on only part of a composite key. Here `course_title` and `instructor_name` depend on `section_id` alone, so they belong in a sections table, leaving `grade` with the full key.
hints: Look at which columns depend on the whole key and which depend on a part of it.
1NF is about atomic values, 2NF about partial dependencies, 3NF about transitive dependencies.
